unit: S: flexible authorization model (users, groups, roles, policies)
title: Hundreds of projects; teams touch only resources tagged with their project
must_teach: Correct: ABAC - a single policy with Condition StringEquals aws:ResourceTag/project = aws:PrincipalTag/project, with tags set on roles/Identity Center attributes and enforced on resource creation. New projects need no new policies.
distractor_angles: one IAM group and policy per project listing ARNs (does not scale, policy size limits); one account per project (plausible but heavy; not 'least change'); permissions boundary per project (caps, does not grant by tag); SCP per project (SCPs are account-level)

unit: S: security strategy for multiple accounts (Control Tower, SCPs)
title: New company: 20 accounts with guardrails and self-service account creation
must_teach: Correct: Control Tower - landing zone with log archive and audit accounts, controls, and Account Factory. Plain Organizations needs you to hand-build all of it.
distractor_angles: Organizations with hand-written SCPs and StackSets (works, more ops); Service Catalog alone (only provisioning); Config aggregator plus Security Hub (detective only, no account vending); one account with separate VPCs (violates blast-radius requirement)

unit: S: appropriate use of resource policies
title: Role in account B must read a bucket in account A - minimal correct change
must_teach: Correct: bucket policy in A allowing the B role ARN, plus the B role's identity policy allowing s3:GetObject on that bucket; set Object Ownership to bucket owner enforced so uploaded objects are readable. One side alone fails cross-account.
distractor_angles: only an identity policy in B (cross-account needs the resource side); make the bucket public and rely on Block Public Access being off (over-exposed); create an IAM user in A and share keys (long-lived keys); object ACLs per object (legacy, does not scale)

unit: S: flexible authorization model (users, groups, roles, policies)
title: 50 developers need identical permissions, new hires must be onboarded quickly - least ops
must_teach: Correct: put users in an IAM group with a customer-managed policy (or better, an Identity Center group with a permission set). Groups cannot be nested and cannot be principals in resource policies.
distractor_angles: inline policy copied to each user (does not scale); one shared IAM user (violates individual accountability); nested groups (do not exist); resource policies listing each user (wrong policy type)

unit: S: best practices for IAM users and root users (MFA)
title: Require MFA before IAM users can terminate instances or delete buckets
must_teach: Correct: identity policy (or permissions boundary) with Condition Bool aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent true on the destructive actions. Trap: putting the same condition in an SCP blocks service roles that never have MFA context.
distractor_angles: SCP denying all actions without MFA (violates constraint: breaks workload roles); strengthen the password policy (wrong feature); CloudTrail + EventBridge alert on terminate (detective only); require MFA only at console sign-in (does not cover CLI/API)

unit: S: role-based access control strategy (STS, role switching, cross-account)
title: Central identity account, users switch into dev/prod accounts - what must exist where
must_teach: Correct: a role in each target account whose trust policy allows the identity account (or its specific principals) plus an identity policy in the identity account allowing sts:AssumeRole on those role ARNs. SCPs and resource policies do not create this path.
distractor_angles: duplicate IAM users in every account (violates single identity); an SCP that grants access to prod (SCPs never grant); resource policies on every service (unworkable); Identity Center enabled but no permission set assignments (right service, incomplete)

unit: S: when to federate a directory service with IAM roles
title: On-prem AD, 15 accounts, no directory data may be stored in AWS - workforce SSO design
must_teach: Correct: IAM Identity Center with AD Connector (over VPN/DX) as the identity source and permission sets per group. Managed Microsoft AD with a trust stores directory data in AWS; Simple AD cannot trust; Cognito is for customers.
distractor_angles: Managed Microsoft AD with a two-way trust (violates 'no directory data in AWS'); Simple AD synced by script (no trust, no MFA); Cognito user pool with SAML (customer identity tool); IAM users created by a sync job (long-lived credentials)

unit: S: flexible authorization model (users, groups, roles, policies)
title: Reusable permission set updated in one place vs a one-off permission tied to a single role
must_teach: Correct: customer-managed policy for the reusable set (versioned, attach to many roles, edit once), inline policy for the strict one-to-one permission that must die with the role; AWS-managed policies cannot be edited.
distractor_angles: edit the AWS managed policy (impossible); inline policy copied into every role (no central update); resource policy on each service (wrong policy type); permissions boundary (caps rather than grants)

unit: S: security strategy for multiple accounts (Control Tower, SCPs)
title: No member principal, even root, can stop logging or leave the org - choose two
must_teach: Correct pair: (1) SCP at the root denying cloudtrail:StopLogging/DeleteTrail/UpdateTrail and organizations:LeaveOrganization; (2) an organization trail owned by the management account writing to a central bucket. IAM policies cannot bind root; Config and log validation are detective/integrity only.
distractor_angles: IAM deny policy on root in each member account (root ignores IAM); attach the SCP to the management account (no effect); Config rule cloudtrail-enabled with remediation (detective, can be raced); enable log file validation (integrity, not prevention)

unit: S: role-based access control strategy (STS, role switching, cross-account)
title: Ten-hour job assumes a role from another role and dies after one hour - fix
must_teach: Correct: role chaining caps sessions at 1 hour regardless of MaxSessionDuration; have the compute's own role (instance profile/task role) be trusted directly by the target role and set MaxSessionDuration up to 12 hours, or make the job re-assume and refresh credentials.
distractor_angles: raise MaxSessionDuration on the chained role to 12 h (ignored for chaining); use GetSessionToken (only for IAM users); switch to an IAM user with keys (violates best practice); add DurationSeconds=43200 to the AssumeRole call (rejected for chained sessions)

unit: S: best practices for IAM users and root users (MFA)
title: Audit finds root has access keys and no MFA - most secure remediation
must_teach: Correct: enable hardware/virtual MFA on root, delete the root access keys, and move daily work to Identity Center/roles. Root cannot be limited by IAM policies; only an SCP limits root in member accounts.
distractor_angles: attach a restrictive IAM policy to root (violates: IAM policies do not apply to root); rotate the root access keys (right idea, wrong control - keys should not exist); create an admin IAM user with long-lived keys instead (violates best practice); enable CloudTrail alarms only (detective, not preventive)

unit: S: security strategy for multiple accounts (Control Tower, SCPs)
title: Stop member accounts creating resources outside eu-west-1, global services intact
must_teach: Correct: SCP on the root/OU that denies actions when aws:RequestedRegion is not eu-west-1, with NotAction excluding global services (IAM, Organizations, Route 53, CloudFront, STS, Support). Control Tower's Region deny control is this SCP under the hood.
distractor_angles: IAM policy in each account (admins can edit it; does not bind root); Config rule flagging non-EU resources (detective only); Service Quotas set to zero in other Regions (not possible for all services); disable other Regions in each account (opt-in Regions only, not the default ones)

unit: S: appropriate use of resource policies
title: S3 in account A must publish to SNS/Lambda in account B - which policy
must_teach: Correct: resource-based policy on the target (SNS topic policy / Lambda resource policy) allowing the s3.amazonaws.com service principal with aws:SourceAccount/aws:SourceArn conditions. Service principals do not assume roles for notifications.
distractor_angles: identity policy attached to 'S3' (services have no identity policy); create a role that S3 assumes (event notifications do not use roles); SCP allowing cross-account SNS (SCPs never grant); Lambda execution role granting S3 access (wrong direction)

unit: S: role-based access control strategy (STS, role switching, cross-account)
title: SaaS monitoring vendor needs read access to your account - most secure
must_teach: Correct: cross-account IAM role with a trust policy naming the vendor account and a Condition on sts:ExternalId; vendor calls AssumeRole and gets temporary credentials.
distractor_angles: create an IAM user and email access keys (long-lived keys); make the resources public with a resource policy (over-exposed); Identity Center user for the vendor (workforce tool, still a human login); trust the vendor account without external ID (confused deputy)

unit: S: when to federate a directory service with IAM roles
title: Mobile users sign in with Google and must upload to their own S3 prefix - which federation
must_teach: Correct: Cognito identity pool exchanging the Google token for temporary credentials of a role scoped with ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub} in the resource ARN. Identity Center and SAML-to-IAM are for workforce; IAM users per app user is wrong.
distractor_angles: IAM Identity Center users for customers (workforce tool); SAML federation into IAM (enterprise IdP, not Google consumer); IAM user per customer (keys on devices); presigned URLs generated with a shared key baked into the app (credential leak)

title: Control Tower: landing zone, guardrails (controls), Account Factory
must_teach: Control Tower builds a multi-account landing zone on Organizations: log archive and audit accounts, preventive controls (SCPs), detective controls (Config rules), proactive controls (CloudFormation hooks), and Account Factory for vending accounts. Choose it for a new multi-account setup with governance; choose plain Organizations when you already have a custom structure or need only SCPs.

title: Directory Service: Managed Microsoft AD vs AD Connector vs Simple AD
must_teach: Managed Microsoft AD = real AD in AWS, supports trusts with on-prem AD, MFA via RADIUS, needed for FSx/RDS SQL Server/WorkSpaces at scale. AD Connector = proxy to on-prem AD, no data in the cloud, needs VPN/DX, no trust. Simple AD = Samba-based, small, no trust/MFA. Identity Center can use any of the first two as identity source.

unit: R2 service: AWS IAM Identity Center
title: IAM Identity Center: workforce SSO with permission sets across Organization accounts
must_teach: Identity Center is the successor to AWS SSO: connect an identity source (its own store, Managed AD/AD Connector, or an external SAML/SCIM IdP), assign permission sets (which become roles in each account) to users/groups, and give people one access portal and CLI SSO. Choose it over IAM users or per-account SAML for any multi-account workforce.

title: IAM: global identity service - users, groups, roles, policy types, evaluation logic, ABAC
must_teach: IAM is global and free: users (humans with passwords/keys, avoid), groups (attach policies to many users), roles (assumed by services, federated identities or other accounts; temporary credentials), and policies (identity-based, resource-based, permissions boundaries, SCPs, session policies). Evaluation: explicit deny > SCP/boundary allow needed > explicit allow; default deny. Tag conditions enable ABAC.
gap_note: Live card covers only roles vs users; the service card must give the full object model, policy types and the evaluation summary.

title: Organizations: OUs, SCPs, consolidated billing, delegated administrators
must_teach: Organizations gives one management account, OUs, SCPs, consolidated billing with shared RI/Savings Plan discounts and volume tiers, and delegated admin for services like GuardDuty and Security Hub. Management account is exempt from SCPs; SCPs filter but never grant; all-features mode is required for SCPs and tag policies.
gap_note: Live card covers SCP evaluation only; the service card must add OUs, billing benefits, delegated admin, all-features mode.

unit: R2 service: AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM)
title: RAM: share subnets, Transit Gateways, Route 53 Resolver rules, licenses across accounts
must_teach: RAM shares resources (VPC subnets, TGW, Resolver rules, License Manager configs, Outposts) with accounts or OUs so resources exist once; sharing within an Organization needs no acceptance. Choose it over duplicating VPCs; it does not share S3 buckets or IAM roles (those use resource policies).

unit: K: AWS federated access and identity services (IAM, IAM Identity Center)
title: Federation options: IAM SAML/OIDC, Identity Center, Cognito - which identity for whom
must_teach: Workforce users go through IAM Identity Center (SAML/SCIM from Okta/Entra/AD) or a SAML 2.0 provider in IAM (AssumeRoleWithSAML, single account); customer/app users go through Cognito (AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity). In all cases the identity ends up in an IAM role with temporary STS credentials - no IAM users are created for federated people.
gap_note: Live card covers Identity Center for multi-account SSO only; missing the IAM SAML provider path for a single account and the Cognito path for customer identities.

unit: K: AWS global infrastructure (Availability Zones, Regions)
title: Regions, AZs and edge as security and residency boundaries
must_teach: A Region is the data-residency boundary: data never leaves it unless you replicate it; AZs are isolated fault domains inside it. IAM, Organizations, Route 53, CloudFront and WAF (for CloudFront) are global; KMS keys, ACM certificates, VPCs and most resources are Regional. To pin a company to one Region, use an SCP with aws:RequestedRegion, not IAM policies per account.

unit: K: Access controls and management across multiple accounts
title: Layers of multi-account access control: OU/SCP, cross-account roles, Identity Center, RAM
must_teach: Four layers stack: Organizations OUs carry SCPs (guardrails, never grants), cross-account IAM roles carry the actual permissions, IAM Identity Center hands humans permission sets in every account, and RAM shares resources (subnets, TGW) without copying them. Rule: prevent with SCP, grant with roles, share with RAM.
gap_note: Live card only explains SCP evaluation; the concept card must lay out the four layers and which one to reach for per requirement.

unit: K: AWS security best practices (principle of least privilege)
title: The exam's security-best-practice checklist: roles over keys, MFA, least privilege, audit
must_teach: Checklist the exam expects: lock and MFA the root user with no access keys; humans sign in through Identity Center, workloads use roles (instance profiles, task roles, execution roles), never embedded keys; grant least privilege with conditions; rotate credentials; log everything with CloudTrail; encrypt by default. Whenever an option mentions long-lived access keys on a server, it is the wrong option.

unit: K: The AWS shared responsibility model
title: Shared responsibility: OF the cloud vs IN the cloud, and how the line moves by service
must_teach: AWS secures the infrastructure (hardware, facilities, hypervisor, managed-service patching); the customer secures what they put in it (data, IAM, OS patching on EC2, security groups, encryption choices). The line moves: on EC2 you patch the OS, on RDS AWS patches the engine but you set encryption and access, on Lambda/S3 you own only data, code and permissions.

unit: R3 pattern: IAM Access Analyzer and credential report
title: Access Analyzer (external/unused access, policy checks) vs IAM credential report
must_teach: Access Analyzer finds resources reachable from outside the zone of trust (S3, KMS, roles, SQS, secrets...) and unused roles/keys and validates/generates policies; the credential report is a CSV of every IAM user's password/key age and MFA state.

title: Permissions boundaries: let developers create roles without escalating privilege
must_teach: A permissions boundary is a managed policy that caps the maximum permissions of a user or role; combine with iam:PermissionsBoundary condition so developers can only create roles that carry the boundary. It never grants; it is the per-identity twin of an SCP.

unit: R3 pattern: IAM policy evaluation logic
title: Policy evaluation: explicit deny, SCP, boundary, session, allow, default deny
must_teach: Every request is denied by default; an explicit Deny anywhere wins; then SCPs, permissions boundaries and session policies must allow; then an identity-based or (same-account) resource-based Allow is needed. AdministratorAccess cannot override an SCP deny.

unit: R3 pattern: IAM users, groups, roles, and policies
title: The six policy types and which question each answers
must_teach: Identity-based (what can this principal do), resource-based (who can touch this resource; enables cross-account without a role), permissions boundary (cap on an identity), SCP (cap on an account), session policy (cap on one AssumeRole session), ACL (legacy S3). Effective permission = intersection of all caps AND (identity OR resource allow), minus any explicit deny.
gap_note: Live card covers evaluation order with SCP; missing the six-type taxonomy and the cap-vs-grant distinction.

unit: R3 pattern: the principle of least privilege
title: Least privilege: deny by default, scope ARNs and conditions, prune with Access Analyzer
must_teach: Start with no permissions, grant specific actions on specific ARNs with conditions (source VPC, tags, MFA), avoid wildcards and AdministratorAccess, and prune with IAM Access Analyzer policy generation and last-accessed data. Option-scanning rule: the answer that names exact actions/resources beats the one that attaches a broad managed policy.

title: MFA: device types, enforcing it on root and users, aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent, MFA delete
must_teach: MFA types: virtual TOTP, FIDO security key, hardware TOTP. Root and every IAM user should have it; enforce it on API actions with a Condition on aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent (trap: roles used by services have no MFA context, so do not put that condition in SCPs that also hit workloads); S3 MFA delete needs the root user and CLI. Identity Center and Cognito bring their own MFA.

title: SCPs: guardrails that cap, never grant; inheritance through OUs; management account exempt
must_teach: SCPs apply to every principal in member accounts including root; they filter (deny-list or allow-list) but grant nothing, inherit down the OU tree, and never affect the management account or service-linked roles. A user still needs an IAM allow.

unit: R3 pattern: resource policies for AWS services
title: Resource-based policies: bucket policy plus identity policy for cross-account access
must_teach: Cross-account S3 access needs the bucket owner's bucket policy to allow the foreign principal and the caller's identity policy to allow the action; same-account access needs either. Object Ownership 'bucket owner enforced' removes ACL surprises.

title: Cross-account roles: trust policy, external ID for third parties, no shared keys
must_teach: Create a role in the resource account whose trust policy names the partner account (and an ExternalId to prevent the confused deputy), and let the partner AssumeRole; never hand out IAM user keys. Same pattern for your own accounts without the external ID.
gap_note: absorbs aws-role-switching-pattern: Two-allow rule (trust policy + sts:AssumeRole identity allow) is the live cross-

title: STS APIs and session rules: AssumeRole variants, GetSessionToken, durations
must_teach: STS issues temporary credentials: AssumeRole (roles, cross-account), AssumeRoleWithSAML (enterprise IdP), AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity (Cognito/OIDC), GetSessionToken (MFA-protected calls for IAM users), GetFederationToken (legacy broker). Sessions last 15 minutes to 12 hours (role MaxSessionDuration), but role chaining is capped at 1 hour. Credentials cannot be revoked early except by a policy with aws:TokenIssueTime.

unit: S: network segmentation strategies (public and private subnets)
title: Web servers have public IPs; must not be reachable directly but still patch
must_teach: Correct: internet-facing ALB in public subnets, EC2 in private subnets without public IPs, egress for patches via NAT gateway (or SSM/patch endpoints). The instances keep working through the ALB.
distractor_angles: keep public IPs but tighten the SG to the ALB (still addressable); move instances to private subnets and add an IGW route (makes them public again); use Elastic IPs (still public); put instances in an isolated subnet with no NAT (breaks patching)

unit: S: VPC architectures with security components (SG, route tables, NACLs, NAT)
title: One IP is attacking instances with public IPs (no ALB) - block it fastest
must_teach: Correct: add a low-numbered Deny rule for that /32 to the subnet's NACL. Security groups cannot deny; WAF needs CloudFront/ALB/API Gateway in front; route tables act on destinations.
distractor_angles: security group deny rule (does not exist); WAF IP set (no supported resource in front); blackhole route (routes are destination based); Shield Advanced (DDoS, not one IP)

unit: S: securing external network connections (VPN, Direct Connect)
title: Remote employees need access to private VPC apps with AD credentials and MFA - least ops
must_teach: Correct: AWS Client VPN endpoint with Active Directory (or SAML/Identity Center) authentication, MFA, and authorization rules per group; associated with private subnets.
distractor_angles: Site-to-Site VPN from each home (site, not user); bastion host with public SSH and keys (violates best practice); Direct Connect to each employee (impossible); Session Manager only (shell to EC2, not general app access)

unit: S: integrating AWS services to secure applications (Shield, WAF, Identity Center, Secrets Manager)
title: RDS password must rotate every 30 days with no custom code - least ops
must_teach: Correct: Secrets Manager with managed rotation for RDS (built-in Lambda rotator); app fetches the secret at runtime via its role. Parameter Store has no native rotation; KMS stores keys, not secrets.
distractor_angles: Parameter Store SecureString with a scheduled Lambda you write (custom code); store in KMS (KMS does not store secrets); environment variables updated by a pipeline (manual, exposed); IAM DB authentication (valid alternative in some stems, but not 'rotate the password')

unit: S: securing external network connections (VPN, Direct Connect)
title: Regulator requires encryption of all traffic on the Direct Connect link - most secure
must_teach: Correct: IPsec Site-to-Site VPN over a Direct Connect public VIF (or MACsec on a dedicated 10/100 Gbps connection). A private VIF alone is isolated but not encrypted; application TLS covers only some flows.
distractor_angles: use a private VIF (isolation, no encryption); rely on TLS in applications (does not cover all protocols); Client VPN (for users, not sites); PrivateLink over DX (private path, not link encryption)

unit: S: integrating AWS services to secure applications (Shield, WAF, Identity Center, Secrets Manager)
title: Same web ACL on every ALB in 40 accounts, including future ALBs - least ops
must_teach: Correct: Firewall Manager WAF policy from the delegated admin account (requires Organizations and Config); it auto-associates the web ACL with in-scope resources as they appear.
distractor_angles: CloudFormation StackSets deploying web ACLs (does not associate future ALBs); SCP requiring WAF (SCPs cannot enforce associations); Security Hub control (detective); Config rule with remediation per account (works but per-account setup, more ops)

unit: S: network segmentation strategies (public and private subnets)
title: Prod and dev must have separate blast radius, billing and guardrails - what boundary
must_teach: Correct: separate AWS accounts under Organizations (SCPs, billing, IAM boundary), with VPCs per account; subnets and security groups only segment networks, not identities or bills.
distractor_angles: separate subnets in one VPC (network only); separate security groups (host only); separate Regions in one account (same IAM/billing boundary); tag-based ABAC in one account (does not bound blast radius or bills)

unit: S: VPC architectures with security components (SG, route tables, NACLs, NAT)
title: Custom NACL allows 443 inbound but clients time out; SG is fine - fix
must_teach: Correct: NACLs are stateless; add an outbound allow for ephemeral ports 1024-65535 (and inbound ephemeral for outbound-initiated flows). Security groups already handle return traffic statefully.
distractor_angles: add an outbound rule to the security group (already stateful); add inbound port 80 (wrong direction/port); lower the rule number of the 443 rule (order is not the issue); change the route table (routing is fine)

unit: S: VPC architectures with security components (SG, route tables, NACLs, NAT)
title: Three AZs share one NAT gateway; AZ outage cut egress - most available fix
must_teach: Correct: one NAT gateway per AZ with a route table per private subnet pointing at its local NAT. Cross-AZ NAT also incurs data transfer charges.
distractor_angles: second NAT gateway in the same AZ (same failure domain); NAT instances in an ASG (more ops, still cross-AZ); attach the IGW route to private subnets (makes them public); replace with interface endpoints for everything (only covers AWS services)
gap_note: overlaps aws-single-nat-gateway-spof-mcq-31: write it from a different angle/scenario (Identical stem (one NAT in one AZ, AZ outage cuts egress), identical a)

unit: S: VPC architectures with security components (SG, route tables, NACLs, NAT)
title: Private instances need only S3 and DynamoDB, no internet - least cost
must_teach: Correct: gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB (free, route-table entries). NAT gateway and interface endpoints both cost hourly plus per GB.
distractor_angles: NAT gateway (hourly + per-GB); interface endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB (works, but hourly per AZ); IGW with public IPs (violates no-internet); Transit Gateway to a shared egress VPC (heavy and paid)
gap_note: moved: A least-cost qualifier in the security domain duplicates aws-d4-transfer-cost-ro

unit: S: network segmentation strategies (public and private subnets)
title: RDS instance is publicly accessible and reachable from the internet - most secure fix
must_teach: Correct: place it in a DB subnet group of private/isolated subnets, set Publicly Accessible = No, and restrict the SG to the app tier SG. Encryption, IAM auth and WAF do not remove network exposure.
distractor_angles: keep public but add a NACL deny for 0.0.0.0/0 on 3306 (still public, brittle); enable encryption at rest (does not affect reachability); enable IAM DB authentication (auth, not exposure); put WAF in front (WAF cannot front RDS)

unit: S: appropriate use of resource policies
title: Instances reach only company buckets; buckets accept only VPC traffic
must_teach: Correct: gateway endpoint policy restricting Resource to the company bucket ARNs plus a bucket policy Deny with Condition StringNotEquals aws:sourceVpce. Gateway endpoints have no security group; instances have no NAT so aws:SourceIp is wrong.
distractor_angles: security group on the gateway endpoint (does not exist); bucket policy on aws:SourceIp of the NAT gateway (no NAT in design; public IP based); IAM policy on the instance role alone (does not stop other principals); NACL allowing only S3 IP ranges (does not scope buckets)
gap_note: moved: The decision is gateway-endpoint policy plus aws:sourceVpce; the exam guide list

unit: S: integrating AWS services to secure applications (Shield, WAF, Identity Center, Secrets Manager)
title: Need DDoS cost protection, 24/7 response team and L7 visibility - which tier
must_teach: Correct: Shield Advanced (subscription, includes WAF costs for protected resources, SRT, cost credits for scaling during attacks). Shield Standard gives none of those; WAF alone gives L7 rules only.
distractor_angles: Shield Standard (no SRT/cost protection); WAF only (no DDoS cost credits); GuardDuty (detection, not mitigation); Firewall Manager alone (deploys policies; still needs Shield Advanced)

unit: S: VPC architectures with security components (SG, route tables, NACLs, NAT)
title: Web/app/DB tiers behind an ALB - most secure security-group design
must_teach: Correct: ALB SG allows 443 from 0.0.0.0/0; web SG allows 80/443 only from the ALB SG; DB SG allows 3306 only from the app SG; SG-to-SG references, no CIDRs, no 0.0.0.0/0 on the DB.
distractor_angles: DB SG allows 3306 from the VPC CIDR (wider than needed); one SG for all tiers allowing all internal traffic (no segmentation); NACL-only design (stateless, no resource references); DB SG allows app subnet CIDR (breaks when tiers scale or move)

unit: S: securing external network connections (VPN, Direct Connect)
title: Customer-gateway failure took the VPN site offline - most available design
must_teach: Correct: second customer gateway device with its own Site-to-Site VPN connection (each already has two tunnels to two AWS endpoints); or DX with VPN backup. A second VGW is not possible per VPC.
distractor_angles: add a second tunnel to the existing connection (already has two; same CGW); attach a second virtual private gateway (one per VPC); Accelerated VPN (performance, not CGW redundancy); Client VPN as backup (users, not site)

unit: S: integrating AWS services to secure applications (Shield, WAF, Identity Center, Secrets Manager)
title: SQL injection against an API behind an NLB - change that enables WAF
must_teach: Correct: WAF attaches to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync and Cognito, not NLB; put CloudFront (or replace NLB with ALB) in front and attach the web ACL there. Shield Advanced on NLB handles DDoS, not injection.
distractor_angles: attach WAF directly to the NLB (unsupported); Shield Advanced on the NLB (DDoS only); security-group rules on port 443 (no L7 inspection); GuardDuty (detects, does not block)

unit: S: integrating AWS services to secure applications (Shield, WAF, Identity Center, Secrets Manager)
title: HTTP flood from thousands of rotating IPs against an ALB - least ops mitigation
must_teach: Correct: WAF web ACL on the ALB with a rate-based rule (requests per 5 minutes per IP) plus the Bot Control managed rule group; optionally CloudFront in front. Shield Standard already covers L3/4; NACLs cannot keep up with rotating IPs.
distractor_angles: NACL deny rules per IP (unmanageable); Shield Standard (already on, L3/4 only); scale the ASG bigger (absorbs cost, no mitigation); security group rule limits (allow-only)

title: Client VPN: managed OpenVPN for remote users with AD/SAML/certificate auth
must_teach: Client VPN is the managed OpenVPN endpoint for people (not sites): authenticates with Active Directory, SAML (Identity Center/Okta) or mutual TLS certificates, supports MFA, authorization rules per group, and split tunnel. Choose it for remote staff reaching private resources; choose Site-to-Site VPN for office-to-VPC, Session Manager when only EC2 shell access is needed.

title: Cognito: user pools (auth, hosted UI, MFA, IdPs) vs identity pools (AWS credentials)
must_teach: User pools authenticate app users and return JWTs (hosted UI, MFA, social and SAML IdPs, Lambda triggers); identity pools exchange any identity (user pool, Google, SAML, unauthenticated guests) for temporary IAM credentials via STS. Customer-facing apps only: workforce SSO is Identity Center.

title: Detective: investigate GuardDuty/Security Hub findings with a behaviour graph
must_teach: Detective ingests CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and GuardDuty findings into a graph so you can answer 'what else did this principal/IP touch and since when'. It is the post-alert investigation tool; it does not detect (GuardDuty), scan (Inspector) or aggregate (Security Hub).

title: Direct Connect: dedicated/hosted, VIF types, DX Gateway, unencrypted by default
must_teach: DX is a private physical link (dedicated 1/10/100 Gbps or hosted sub-1 Gbps) with weeks of lead time; private VIF to a VGW/DX Gateway, transit VIF to TGW, public VIF for public AWS endpoints. Traffic is not encrypted: add VPN over DX or MACsec. Resilience needs a second connection or VPN backup.

title: Firewall Manager: org-wide WAF, Shield Advanced, SG and Network Firewall enforcement
must_teach: Firewall Manager applies WAF web ACLs, Shield Advanced protection, security-group baselines and Network Firewall/Route 53 DNS Firewall policies to every matching resource across an Organization, including resources created later. Requires Organizations, a delegated admin account and Config enabled. Choose it when the stem says 'all accounts' and 'automatically for new resources'.

title: GuardDuty: agentless threat detection from CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs; org-wide
must_teach: GuardDuty analyses CloudTrail events, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs plus optional S3, EKS, RDS login, Lambda and malware protection to produce findings (compromised credentials, crypto mining, unusual API calls) without agents; enable org-wide with a delegated admin; route findings to EventBridge for automated response. Not a vulnerability scanner and not a firewall.

title: Inspector: continuous vulnerability and reachability scanning of EC2, ECR, Lambda
must_teach: Inspector automatically scans EC2 (via SSM agent), container images in ECR and Lambda functions for CVEs and unintended network exposure, scoring findings and sending them to Security Hub/EventBridge. Choose it for 'unpatched software' or 'known vulnerabilities'; not for threats (GuardDuty) or data (Macie).

title: Network Firewall: managed VPC firewall with domain filtering and Suricata IPS rules
must_teach: Network Firewall sits in its own subnet as a Gateway Load Balancer-style endpoint that route tables steer traffic through; it filters by domain name, Suricata IPS rules, protocols and IP sets, and is often centralised in an inspection VPC via Transit Gateway. Choose it for egress domain allow-lists or IDS/IPS; security groups and NACLs cannot filter by domain, WAF is HTTP-only.

title: PrivateLink: expose or consume a service privately without peering or CIDR clashes
must_teach: PrivateLink puts a service behind an NLB (or GWLB) as an endpoint service; consumers create interface endpoints in their own VPC. Only the consumer initiates, overlapping CIDRs are fine, and it scales to thousands of consumer VPCs; use peering/TGW when both sides must initiate.

title: Secrets Manager: KMS-encrypted secrets with managed rotation and cross-account access
must_teach: Secrets Manager stores secrets encrypted with KMS, rotates them with built-in Lambda rotators for RDS/Redshift/DocumentDB or custom Lambdas, supports resource policies for cross-account access and replication to other Regions; charged per secret and per API call. Parameter Store SecureString is the free alternative without rotation.

title: Shield Standard vs Advanced: free L3/4 protection vs paid SRT, cost protection, WAF
must_teach: Shield Standard is free and always on for every AWS customer at L3/L4. Shield Advanced ($3,000/month, 1-year commitment) adds near-real-time visibility, 24/7 DDoS Response Team, DDoS cost protection (scaling credits), WAF at no extra charge and health-based detection for EC2/EIP, ELB, CloudFront, Global Accelerator and Route 53. Choose Advanced only when the stem names SRT, cost protection or L7 DDoS on those resources.

title: Site-to-Site VPN: IPsec over the internet, two tunnels, VGW or TGW attachment
must_teach: Site-to-Site VPN is IPsec from a customer gateway to a virtual private gateway or Transit Gateway: minutes to set up, encrypted, about 1.25 Gbps per tunnel, two tunnels per connection for AZ redundancy; add a second customer gateway for on-prem redundancy, Accelerated VPN for consistent global paths. Choose DX for bandwidth/consistency, VPN for speed of setup, encryption or DX backup.

title: Systems Manager: Session Manager, Run Command, Patch Manager, Parameter Store, Automation
must_teach: SSM manages EC2 and on-prem servers through the agent and an instance role: Session Manager (no SSH, logged shells), Run Command, Patch Manager with maintenance windows, Parameter Store for config/secrets, Automation for runbooks (used by Config remediation). Not a monitoring service and not a secret-rotation service.

title: VPC basics: CIDR, subnets per AZ, IGW, route tables, DNS attributes, limits
must_teach: A VPC is a Regional private network with a /16 to /28 CIDR (plus secondary CIDRs); subnets are AZ-bound and get a route table; an Internet Gateway plus a 0.0.0.0/0 route makes a subnet public; enableDnsHostnames/Support are needed for private hosted zones and interface endpoints. Five reserved IPs per subnet, default limit 5 VPCs per Region. Everything in D1 networking hangs off this model.

title: WAF: web ACLs, managed rules, rate-based rules; CloudFront/ALB/API GW/AppSync only
must_teach: WAF filters HTTP(S) requests with web ACLs made of AWS managed rule groups (SQLi, XSS, bot control, IP reputation), custom rules (geo, headers, IP sets) and rate-based rules; it attaches to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync, Cognito user pools and App Runner, never to NLB or EC2 directly. Priced per web ACL, rule and million requests.

unit: K: Application configuration and credentials security
title: Where app secrets belong: roles, Secrets Manager, Parameter Store, IMDSv2
must_teach: Never store credentials in code, AMIs, user data or env files in a repo. Give compute an IAM role (credentials delivered via IMDSv2 on EC2, task role on ECS, execution role on Lambda), keep third-party secrets in Secrets Manager (rotation) or Parameter Store SecureString (cheap, no rotation), and fetch at runtime with KMS-encrypted values.

unit: K: Security services with appropriate use cases (Cognito, GuardDuty, Macie)
title: Security-service picker: GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Detective, Security Hub, Cognito
must_teach: GuardDuty = threat detection from logs (no agents); Inspector = vulnerability scanning of EC2/ECR/Lambda; Macie = sensitive data in S3; Detective = investigate findings; Security Hub = aggregate and score; Cognito = customer sign-in. The trigger words in the stem (threat, CVE, PII, root cause, compliance score, user sign-up) pick the service.

unit: K: Control ports, protocols, and network traffic on AWS
title: Layered traffic control: route table, NACL, security group, host, Network Firewall
must_teach: Traffic is decided in order by route table (can it get there), NACL at the subnet (stateless, allow and deny, numbered), security group at the ENI (stateful, allow only), then the OS firewall; Network Firewall adds domain/IPS filtering at the VPC edge and WAF at HTTP layer. Match the requirement to the layer: block an IP = NACL, restrict by source resource = SG referencing, restrict domains = Network Firewall.

title: Front-door, admin and object-level access patterns for applications
must_teach: User access: Cognito user pool or ALB/API Gateway authentication before requests reach compute. Admin access: Session Manager instead of SSH/bastions. Object access: presigned URLs or CloudFront signed URLs/OAC instead of public buckets. Service-to-service: IAM roles and VPC endpoints instead of public endpoints.

title: Public, gateway and interface endpoints: private paths to AWS services, locked down
must_teach: Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB only) are free route-table entries usable only from inside the VPC; interface endpoints (PrivateLink) are ENIs with private IPs, hourly cost, reachable from on-premises over VPN/DX. Both accept an endpoint policy; the bucket can require aws:sourceVpce.

unit: K: Threat vectors external to AWS (DDoS, SQL injection)
title: Threat to control: L3/4 flood -> Shield, L7 injection/bots -> WAF, keys -> GuardDuty
must_teach: DDoS at network/transport layer is absorbed by Shield Standard (free, automatic) or Shield Advanced (paid, SRT, cost protection) plus edge services (CloudFront, Route 53, Global Accelerator); SQL injection, XSS, bad bots and HTTP floods are stopped by WAF rules attached to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway or AppSync. Neither runs on NLB or EC2 directly.
gap_note: Quality: mention that WAF cannot attach to NLB and that CloudFront in front is the standard fix.

unit: R3 pattern: ALB authentication with Cognito or OIDC
title: ALB built-in authentication: authenticate-cognito / authenticate-oidc listener rules
must_teach: An HTTPS ALB listener rule can authenticate users against a Cognito user pool or any OIDC IdP before forwarding, passing identity in x-amzn-oidc-* headers; no login code on the targets.

title: API Gateway auth: IAM, Cognito authorizer, Lambda authorizer; API keys are not auth
must_teach: IAM authorisation for AWS callers, Cognito user pool authorizer for app users, Lambda authorizer for custom tokens; API keys with usage plans meter and throttle but do not authenticate; resource policies restrict by IP/VPC/account.

title: DDoS defence in depth: Shield, edge absorption, WAF rate limits, small attack surface
must_teach: Layer it: Shield Standard on everything; put CloudFront/Route 53/Global Accelerator in front so the edge absorbs floods; hide origins in private subnets behind ALB with WAF rate-based rules and bot control; autoscale to absorb; Shield Advanced for cost protection and SRT on high-value apps. Do not answer 'bigger instances' or 'NACL each IP'.

unit: R3 pattern: encrypting Direct Connect traffic
title: DX is unencrypted: VPN over public VIF or MACsec, DX Gateway for multi-Region
must_teach: Direct Connect provides isolation, not encryption; encrypt with an IPsec VPN over a public VIF (VGW/TGW as endpoint) or MACsec on dedicated 10/100 Gbps ports; a DX Gateway reaches VPCs in multiple Regions from one connection.

title: IMDSv2: session-oriented metadata to stop SSRF credential theft
must_teach: Instance role credentials come from the metadata service; IMDSv1 answers any GET so an SSRF bug leaks them. IMDSv2 requires a PUT to get a token with a hop limit and TTL; enforce it with HttpTokens=required at launch or in launch templates and at account level.

title: NACLs: stateless, numbered rules, ephemeral ports, blocking a single IP at the subnet
must_teach: NACLs are stateless subnet filters evaluated by rule number (lowest first, first match wins, implicit deny at *); you must allow return traffic on ephemeral ports 1024-65535 in both directions; default NACL allows all, custom ones deny all. Use them to deny a specific CIDR; do not use them as the primary control (SGs are).

unit: R3 pattern: using public subnets and private subnets
title: Public/private/isolated subnet tiers: what defines each and what goes where
must_teach: A subnet is public only because its route table points 0.0.0.0/0 at an IGW and instances get public IPs; private subnets route egress through NAT; isolated (database) subnets have no internet route at all. Standard three-tier: load balancers/NAT/bastions public, app private, databases isolated, each tier replicated per AZ; Lambda and RDS should never need a public subnet.

title: Route tables: main vs custom, one per subnet, local route, longest prefix, propagation
must_teach: Every subnet uses exactly one route table (main by default); the local route for the VPC CIDR cannot be removed; 0.0.0.0/0 to an IGW makes a subnet public, to a NAT gateway keeps it private with egress, to a VGW/TGW sends on-prem traffic; most specific prefix wins; VGW routes can propagate automatically. Gateway endpoints and peering also live here, so 'cannot reach X' questions often end in a missing route.

unit: R3 pattern: private origin with Origin Access Control
title: Keep S3 private behind CloudFront with OAC so every request passes the edge, WAF and TLS
must_teach: OAC signs CloudFront's origin requests; the bucket policy allows only that distribution's service principal; Block Public Access stays on; SSE-KMS buckets are supported (unlike the old OAI).

title: Presigned URLs: time-limited object access using the signer's permissions
must_teach: A presigned URL carries the signer's credentials and expiry (max 7 days with IAM user keys, session lifetime with roles); the client needs no AWS credentials; it grants exactly one operation on one object. Use for uploads/downloads from apps; use CloudFront signed URLs/cookies for CDN-scale private content.

title: Reference a security group as the source instead of maintaining IP lists
must_teach: Allow the DB port from the app tier's security group ID; membership follows scaling automatically. Works across peered VPCs in the same Region; not across Regions.

title: Injection/OWASP attacks: WAF managed rule groups plus least-privilege data access
must_teach: SQL injection, XSS and path traversal are HTTP-layer attacks: attach WAF with the AWS managed Core (CRS) and SQL database rule groups to CloudFront/ALB/API Gateway; back it with parameterised queries and a DB user that has only the needed rights. Shield, security groups and GuardDuty do not inspect request bodies.

unit: R3 pattern: Session Manager instead of bastion hosts
title: Session Manager: no inbound ports, IAM-controlled, logged shells; replaces bastions
must_teach: With the SSM agent, an instance role and (in private subnets) SSM interface endpoints or NAT, Session Manager gives shell/port-forwarding access with no SSH port, no keys, IAM permissions per instance tag, and session logs to S3/CloudWatch.

title: Flow Logs: accepted/rejected 5-tuples per ENI/subnet/VPC; what they cannot show
must_teach: Flow Logs capture metadata (src/dst IP, port, protocol, ACCEPT/REJECT) at VPC, subnet or ENI level into CloudWatch Logs or S3; REJECT rows point at SG/NACL drops; they never contain payloads and skip DNS to the resolver, DHCP, metadata and Windows licence traffic. Use Traffic Mirroring for packets.

title: NAT gateway: managed egress for private subnets, per AZ, no inbound, hourly + per GB
must_teach: A NAT gateway lives in a public subnet and lets private-subnet resources initiate outbound IPv4 traffic; deploy one per AZ with per-AZ route tables for resilience; it never accepts inbound connections; IPv6 uses an egress-only IGW instead; prefer gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB to avoid NAT charges.

title: Security groups: stateful ENI firewall, allow-only, default deny in / allow out
must_teach: Security groups are stateful (return traffic allowed automatically), evaluate all rules, allow only (no deny), attach to ENIs, and can reference other security groups or prefix lists as sources; default SG allows all outbound and inbound only from itself.

unit: S: encrypting data in transit (ACM using TLS)
title: ACM cert issued in ap-southeast-2 cannot be selected on CloudFront - fix
must_teach: Correct: request/import the certificate in us-east-1; CloudFront only reads ACM certs there (ALB/API Gateway use the cert in their own Region).
distractor_angles: request the cert in the distribution's 'Region' (CloudFront is global; us-east-1 specifically); export the cert and install on the origin (ACM public certs are not exportable; origin cert is separate); use ACM Private CA (private certs not trusted by browsers); upload to IAM certificate store (legacy, unnecessary)

unit: S: rotating encryption keys and renewing certificates
title: ACM certificate is 30 days from expiry and has not renewed - most likely cause and fix
must_teach: Correct: ACM auto-renews only DNS-validated (CNAME still present) or email-validated (owner responds) certs that are associated with a resource; imported certificates never auto-renew - re-import or replace with an ACM-issued cert. Check the CNAME record and association first.
distractor_angles: ACM renews imported certificates automatically (false); redeploy the ALB to trigger renewal (no effect); buy a third-party cert every year (ops burden); move to IAM certificate store (legacy, no renewal)

unit: S: aligning AWS technologies to meet compliance requirements
title: Auditor wants AWS's SOC 2 and PCI attestation documents - where
must_teach: Correct: AWS Artifact reports (and agreements such as the BAA). Security Hub, Config and Trusted Advisor describe your posture, not AWS's certifications.
distractor_angles: Security Hub PCI standard (your resources, not AWS's audit); Config conformance pack (your resources); Trusted Advisor security checks (your resources); open a Support case (slower, unnecessary)

unit: S: implementing data backups and replications
title: Central backups for EBS/RDS/DynamoDB/EFS that even an admin cannot delete
must_teach: Correct: AWS Backup plan by tag into a vault with Vault Lock in compliance mode, copied to a second account/Region. Object Lock is S3-only and DLM is EBS-only.
distractor_angles: S3 Object Lock (only S3); Data Lifecycle Manager policies (EBS only, deletable); scripted snapshots with MFA delete (MFA delete is S3 only; scripts deletable); cross-Region snapshot copy without a locked vault (still deletable)

unit: S: aligning AWS technologies to meet compliance requirements
title: Continuously check 50 accounts against CIS benchmark with one dashboard - least ops
must_teach: Correct: Security Hub with the CIS standard enabled org-wide via delegated admin (uses Config underneath). Conformance packs per account work but have no cross-account scoring dashboard without extra setup.
distractor_angles: Config conformance packs deployed per account (more ops, no unified score); Inspector (vulnerabilities only); Macie (S3 data only); AWS Artifact (AWS's reports, not your posture)

unit: S: encrypting data in transit (ACM using TLS)
title: Compliance requires encryption all the way to the instances behind an ALB - most secure
must_teach: Correct: HTTPS listener with an ACM cert on the ALB plus an HTTPS target group (instances present their own cert, self-signed is accepted by ALB), or NLB TLS passthrough for true end-to-end. Private subnets do not equal encryption.
distractor_angles: HTTPS listener with HTTP targets in private subnets (plaintext inside VPC); install the ACM public cert on the instances (not exportable); Site-to-Site VPN inside the VPC (nonsense); restrict the SG to the ALB (access control, not encryption)

unit: S: implementing access policies for encryption keys
title: Security team manages keys but never decrypts; app decrypts but never administers
must_teach: Correct: key policy with two statements - administrators get kms:Create*/Describe*/Enable*/Put*/Update*/Revoke*/Disable*/Get*/List*/ScheduleKeyDeletion/CancelKeyDeletion, users get Encrypt/Decrypt/ReEncrypt*/GenerateDataKey*/DescribeKey; keep 'Enable IAM User Permissions' scoped or removed. AWS-managed keys cannot express this.
distractor_angles: single statement giving both kms:* (no separation); rely on IAM policies with the default key policy (root delegation lets any IAM admin grant themselves use); grants for administrators (grants are for use, not admin); use the AWS-managed aws/s3 key (no editable policy)

unit: S: implementing access policies for encryption keys
title: Account B role must decrypt S3 objects encrypted with a customer-managed key in account A
must_teach: Correct: key policy in A grants kms:Decrypt (and DescribeKey) to account B (root or role), and B's role identity policy allows kms:Decrypt on that key ARN, plus the S3 bucket policy for the object. KMS keys cannot be exported, copied or shared via RAM.
distractor_angles: identity policy in B only (key policy must allow B); bucket policy alone (S3 access without key access still fails); share the key with RAM (unsupported); copy the key to account B (keys are not exportable)

unit: S: rotating encryption keys and renewing certificates
title: Yearly rotation for imported-material and asymmetric keys - approach
must_teach: Correct: automatic rotation is only for symmetric customer-managed keys with KMS-generated material; imported, asymmetric, HMAC and custom-key-store keys need manual rotation: create a new key and repoint the alias, keeping the old key for decrypting existing data. No re-encryption of old data is required.
distractor_angles: enable automatic rotation on the imported-material key (unsupported); re-encrypt all data with the new key (unnecessary; alias swap suffices); delete the old key after rotation (breaks decryption of old ciphertext); switch to an AWS-managed key (loses control; still symmetric only)

unit: S: implementing access policies for encryption keys
title: Key may be used only through S3 in eu-west-1, never by direct API calls
must_teach: Correct: key policy condition kms:ViaService = s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com (and kms:CallerAccount); direct Decrypt calls from users are denied even with the key ARN allowed in IAM.
distractor_angles: aws:SourceIp condition (users in the office still call KMS directly); separate key per service without a condition (does not stop direct calls); grants to the S3 service (grants are created by the service, not a restriction); permissions boundary on users (does not bind service usage)

unit: S: implementing policies for data access, lifecycle, and protection
title: Discover which of 300 buckets contain PII and alert on public exposure - least ops
must_teach: Correct: Macie with automated sensitive-data discovery and bucket policy findings, sending to Security Hub/EventBridge. GuardDuty/Inspector do not read object content.
distractor_angles: GuardDuty S3 protection (threat activity, not content); Inspector (vulnerabilities); Athena scans with regex (custom, manual); Config s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited (exposure only, no PII)

unit: S: implementing policies for data access, lifecycle, and protection
title: Financial records must be undeletable for 7 years even by root - which control
must_teach: Correct: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a 7-year retention period (versioning required). Governance mode can be bypassed with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention; MFA delete and bucket policies can be undone by root/admins.
distractor_angles: governance mode retention (bypassable); versioning plus MFA delete (root can still delete); bucket policy denying s3:DeleteObject (admins change the policy); lifecycle rule with 7-year expiration (expiry is not immutability)

title: Existing unencrypted RDS instance must be encrypted at rest - least downtime path
must_teach: Correct: take a snapshot, copy it with a KMS key, restore from the encrypted copy, cut over (or DMS for near-zero downtime). Encryption cannot be enabled in place and an unencrypted instance cannot have encrypted replicas.
distractor_angles: modify the instance and tick 'encrypt' (not possible); create an encrypted read replica and promote (not possible from unencrypted source); enable EBS encryption by default (does not apply to RDS); enable TDE (only Oracle/SQL Server, still not KMS at-rest for the volume)

unit: S: implementing policies for data access, lifecycle, and protection
title: Hundreds of apps need prefix-level access to one bucket; policy hit size limit
must_teach: Correct: S3 Access Points, one per app/team with its own policy (and optional VPC restriction), delegating from a bucket policy that trusts the access points. Splitting into hundreds of buckets or ACLs is the trap.
distractor_angles: one giant bucket policy (20 KB limit, unmanageable); separate bucket per app (breaks the single data lake); object ACLs (legacy, per-object); presigned URLs per app (temporary, not a policy model)

unit: S: encrypting data in transit (ACM using TLS)
title: Reject any S3 request that is not over HTTPS - least ops
must_teach: Correct: bucket policy Deny s3:* with Condition Bool aws:SecureTransport false (and s3:TlsVersion for minimum TLS). SSE settings cover rest, not transit.
distractor_angles: enable SSE-KMS (at rest); enable Block Public Access (exposure, not transport); require a VPC endpoint (private path, still may be HTTP); attach an ACM cert to the bucket (buckets cannot hold certs)

unit: S: implementing data backups and replications
title: Compliance copy in another Region incl. old objects and deletions - choose two
must_teach: Correct pair: enable versioning on both buckets and create a CRR rule with delete-marker replication; run S3 Batch Replication (or Batch Operations copy) for pre-existing objects. Plain CRR copies only new writes; KMS objects need the key allowed.
distractor_angles: enable CRR only (skips existing objects); Transfer Acceleration (upload speed, not copying); DataSync S3-to-S3 (works but no ongoing replication semantics/delete markers); lifecycle transition to another Region (lifecycle cannot move across Regions)

title: Need per-object decrypt audit trail and ability to revoke access to one dataset's key
must_teach: Correct: SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key (key policy you control, CloudTrail logs each Decrypt); enable S3 Bucket Keys to cut KMS request cost. SSE-S3 and AWS-managed keys give no revocation; SSE-C makes you ship keys.
distractor_angles: SSE-S3 (no per-key audit or revocation); SSE-KMS with the aws/s3 AWS-managed key (cannot edit its policy); SSE-C (client must send key each call); client-side encryption with an app-held key (no CloudTrail decrypt audit)
batch: B1 黄金五张（MCQ，跑通流程）

title: Share an encrypted AMI/snapshot with another account - what must be true
must_teach: Correct: the snapshot must be encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key whose key policy grants the target account kms:DescribeKey/ReEncrypt/CreateGrant/Decrypt; then share the snapshot/AMI with that account (it re-encrypts with its own key). AWS-managed aws/ebs keys cannot be shared; encrypted snapshots cannot be public.
distractor_angles: share as-is with the aws/ebs key (unsupported); make the snapshot public (blocked for encrypted); copy unencrypted then share (violates encryption requirement); use RAM to share the KMS key (RAM does not share KMS keys)

unit: S: best practices for IAM users and root users (MFA)
title: Find users without MFA or with 90-day-old keys across 30 accounts - least ops
must_teach: Correct: Config managed rules (iam-user-mfa-enabled, access-keys-rotated) via an organization aggregator, or the IAM credential report per account; the org-wide, continuous answer is Config/Security Hub. Trusted Advisor covers MFA on root only at Basic tier.
distractor_angles: download credential report from each account monthly (manual, not continuous); CloudTrail Insights (wrong feature: anomalies, not posture); Inspector (wrong service: vulnerabilities); GuardDuty (wrong service: threats)
gap_note: moved: The correct answer is Config managed rules through an org aggregator / Security

title: ACM: free public certificates for ALB/CloudFront/API Gateway, Regional, auto-renewal rules
must_teach: ACM issues free public TLS certificates usable only on integrated services (ALB, NLB TLS, CloudFront, API Gateway, App Runner), never installed on EC2 directly; certificates are Regional except CloudFront which needs us-east-1. Auto-renews DNS-validated certs that are in use; imported certs and email-validated ones need manual renewal. ACM Private CA issues internal certs (paid).

title: AWS Artifact: download AWS compliance reports (SOC, PCI, ISO) and accept agreements (BAA)
must_teach: Artifact is the self-service portal for AWS's own audit reports and certifications and for accepting agreements such as the HIPAA BAA. It says nothing about your workload's compliance; for that use Security Hub standards or Config conformance packs. Trigger phrase: auditor asks for evidence of AWS's compliance.

title: AWS Backup: central backup plans, vaults, Vault Lock, cross-account/cross-Region copy
must_teach: AWS Backup applies backup plans (schedule, retention, lifecycle to cold storage) to EBS, RDS/Aurora, DynamoDB, EFS, FSx, S3, EC2 and more by tag, stores recovery points in vaults, and Vault Lock (compliance mode) makes them undeletable even by admins; copies to other accounts/Regions for DR. Choose it whenever the stem says 'multiple services' or 'central policy' for backups.

title: CloudHSM: single-tenant FIPS 140-2 L3 HSM cluster, your keys, KMS custom key store
must_teach: CloudHSM is a dedicated HSM cluster in your VPC where only you hold the keys (AWS cannot recover them); FIPS 140-2 Level 3, supports PKCS#11/JCE/KSP for Oracle TDE, SSL offload, custom PKI. Use as a KMS custom key store when AWS services must use HSM-held keys. Choose KMS unless the stem says single-tenant, own the HSM, Level 3, or a non-AWS crypto API.

title: CloudTrail: API audit log; organization trail, data vs management events, log integrity
must_teach: CloudTrail records who called which API; management events are on by default (90 days in event history), data events (S3 object, Lambda invoke) and Insights cost extra. Use an organization trail delivering to a locked-down S3 bucket with log file validation for tamper evidence. Not for resource configuration history (Config) or metrics (CloudWatch).

unit: R3 pattern: EBS encryption by default
title: EBS: encryption by default per Region; encrypt existing volumes through snapshot copy
must_teach: Enable 'encryption by default' per Region so every new volume/snapshot copy uses the chosen KMS key; existing unencrypted volumes are fixed by snapshot, copy-with-encryption, create volume, swap. Encrypted snapshots can only be shared with a customer-managed key.

title: Envelope encryption: GenerateDataKey, encrypt locally, store wrapped key with data
must_teach: KMS encrypts at most 4 KB directly, so services call GenerateDataKey, encrypt data locally with the plaintext data key, discard it, and store the KMS-wrapped copy alongside the ciphertext; decrypt reverses it with one KMS call per object.

unit: R3 pattern: access policies for encryption keys
title: KMS key policy vs IAM vs grants; cross-account use; kms:ViaService; admin/user split
must_teach: The key policy is the root of access: the default policy delegates to IAM in the same account ('Enable IAM User Permissions'); without that statement IAM policies do nothing. Cross-account use needs the key policy to allow the external account AND an identity policy there. Grants give services temporary use (EBS, RDS). Separate key administrators (kms:Create*/Put*/Schedule*) from key users (Encrypt/Decrypt/GenerateDataKey); restrict use to a service with kms:ViaService.

title: KMS rotation: which key types rotate automatically; multi-Region keys avoid re-encrypt
must_teach: Automatic rotation (yearly by default, configurable 90-2560 days) applies to customer-managed symmetric keys with KMS-generated material; AWS-managed keys rotate yearly; imported, asymmetric, HMAC and custom-key-store keys need manual rotation via a new key and alias swap. Old material is kept so nothing is re-encrypted. Multi-Region keys share material so a replica Region can decrypt.

unit: R3 pattern: RDS encryption at rest and IAM database authentication
title: RDS: encrypt an existing instance via snapshot copy; IAM DB auth without passwords
must_teach: Encryption cannot be turned on in place: snapshot, copy the snapshot with a KMS key, restore, repoint. Encrypted instances have encrypted replicas/snapshots. IAM database authentication issues 15-minute tokens for MySQL/PostgreSQL so apps use their role instead of a stored password.

unit: R3 pattern: S3 Block Public Access
title: Block Public Access: account and bucket level overrides any public policy or ACL
must_teach: Block Public Access settings at account level override bucket level; when on, PutBucketPolicy with a public grant is rejected and existing public grants are ignored. Turn it off only for the specific bucket that must be public, or better serve it through CloudFront with OAC.

unit: R3 pattern: S3 replication for compliance copies
title: CRR/SRR: versioning both sides, role, Batch Replication for old objects, delete markers
must_teach: Replication requires versioning on source and destination and a role; it copies new objects only, so historic data needs S3 Batch Replication; delete-marker replication is opt-in; KMS-encrypted objects need the key allowed for the role; use Replication Time Control for a 15-minute SLA.

unit: R3 pattern: S3 server-side encryption options
title: SSE-S3 vs SSE-KMS vs SSE-C vs DSSE and client-side: audit, control and cost
must_teach: SSE-S3 is default and free; SSE-KMS adds key policies, CloudTrail per-decrypt audit and revocation but KMS request costs (mitigate with S3 Bucket Keys); SSE-C means you send the key each request; client-side means S3 never sees plaintext. Enforce a choice with a bucket policy on s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption.

title: Object Lock: compliance vs governance mode, retention periods, legal holds
must_teach: Object Lock (needs versioning) makes object versions WORM: compliance mode cannot be shortened or removed by anyone including root until retention ends; governance mode can be bypassed by principals with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention; legal hold is indefinite until removed.

unit: R3 pattern: S3 versioning and MFA delete
title: Versioning makes deletes recoverable; MFA delete requires root plus MFA to purge versions
must_teach: With versioning, a delete adds a delete marker and old versions stay; MFA delete (root user, CLI only) requires an MFA code to permanently delete a version or change the versioning state, so stolen credentials cannot wipe data.

unit: R3 pattern: AWS Certificate Manager [ACM] using TLS
title: TLS everywhere: terminate at the edge, re-encrypt to targets, force TLS on S3/RDS/APIs
must_teach: Terminate TLS with an ACM cert on CloudFront/ALB/NLB/API Gateway; for end-to-end encryption use an HTTPS target group (self-signed certs on instances are accepted by ALB) or NLB TLS passthrough. Force TLS on S3 with a Deny on aws:SecureTransport=false, on RDS with rds.force_ssl / require_secure_transport, and on links with VPN or MACsec. ACM certs never go on EC2.

unit: Determining when to use serverless technologies and patterns
title: Nightly 45-minute batch job, runs once a day; least ops
must_teach: Run it as an ECS Fargate task (or AWS Batch on Fargate) started by an EventBridge Scheduler rule; no host to manage and no runtime ceiling.
distractor_angles: violates constraint: Lambda stops at 15 minutes; violates qualifier: an EC2 instance with cron must be patched and runs idle; plausible but over-engineered: splitting into Lambda chunks orchestrated by Step Functions adds complexity the requirement never asked for

title: Known 9 am spike, reactive scaling too slow; most performant at least cost
must_teach: Add a scheduled scaling action (or predictive scaling) that raises desired capacity before 9 am and lowers it after, keeping target tracking for the rest of the day; capacity is ready before the load arrives.
distractor_angles: violates qualifier: lowering the target-tracking CPU threshold still reacts after load arrives and over-provisions all day; right service wrong feature: a warm pool shortens launch time but still waits for the alarm; violates qualifier: running peak capacity 24x7 meets performance but not cost

title: Worker fleet consuming SQS falls behind; scale on the right metric
must_teach: Target tracking on a custom backlog-per-instance metric (ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible / running instances) so workers scale with queue depth, not CPU.
distractor_angles: right service wrong feature: CPU target tracking misses I/O-bound workers idling while the queue grows; violates constraint: scheduled scaling cannot follow unpredictable producer bursts; wrong metric: step scaling on NetworkIn measures the wrong thing

title: Web tier must not lose orders when slow backend spikes; least ops
must_teach: Put an SQS standard queue between the web tier and worker ASG and scale workers on queue depth; the queue absorbs spikes and retries via visibility timeout, so no order is lost while the backend catches up.

unit: Using purpose-built AWS services for workloads
title: Multi-step order flow with retries and a 2-day human approval; least code
must_teach: Step Functions Standard workflow with Retry/Catch per state and .waitForTaskToken for the approval; execution can pause up to a year.
distractor_angles: violates qualifier: chaining Lambda functions re-implements retries and state; violates constraint: SQS between steps cannot hold a callback token for days without custom bookkeeping; right service wrong feature: Express workflows cap at 5 minutes

title: Reporting queries slow the production RDS writer; least change
must_teach: Create a read replica and point the reporting tool at its endpoint; reads leave the writer with no schema or code change beyond a connection string.
distractor_angles: right service wrong feature: Multi-AZ standby cannot serve reads; violates qualifier: ElastiCache needs application code to read/write the cache; violates qualifier: a larger instance class means a failover/reboot window and does not separate the workloads

unit: How to appropriately use edge accelerators (CDN)

title: Event-driven design: sources, routers, idempotent consumers
must_teach: Producers emit events (S3 notifications, DynamoDB Streams, EventBridge from AWS services and SaaS, application PutEvents); a router (EventBridge rules, SNS) fans them to consumers (Lambda, SQS, Step Functions) that must be idempotent because delivery is at-least-once and ordering is not guaranteed. Benefits: producers never wait or know consumers, spikes are absorbed. Failure handling: retries, DLQs, archive/replay.

title: Scale out vs scale up: when each is the only option
must_teach: Horizontal = add instances/tasks (ASG, ECS service auto scaling, read replicas): no ceiling, no downtime, needs stateless tiers and a load balancer. Vertical = bigger instance/class: has a ceiling, requires a stop/start or RDS failover, but is the only option for a single-writer database or licence-bound app. Decision: stateless -> horizontal; single writer -> vertical or Aurora/global tables.

title: Load balancing for scale: target groups, health checks, ASG attachment
must_teach: A load balancer decouples clients from a fleet: targets register in target groups, only healthy targets get traffic, and attaching the group to an Auto Scaling group makes scale-out invisible to clients. ALB (layer 7) routes per host/path to different microservices; NLB (layer 4) handles millions of TCP/UDP connections with static IPs. Trap: a load balancer does not add capacity, the ASG does.

unit: Design principles for microservices (stateless vs stateful)
title: Microservice principles: stateless, own datastore, async, isolated failure
must_teach: Each service is independently deployable, owns its data store, talks to others through APIs or events not shared tables, and keeps no local session state so any instance can serve any request and be replaced. Stateful pieces (sessions, uploads, locks) move to ElastiCache, DynamoDB, S3 or EFS. Trap: sticky sessions and shared databases are the two ways a design stops being microservices.

title: Three-tier layout: which subnet, which AZ, what sits between tiers
must_teach: Web/app/data tiers live in separate subnets: ALB in public subnets, app ASG in private subnets, database in isolated private subnets, every tier in at least two AZs. Tiers talk through a load balancer or a queue so each scales and fails independently; security groups reference the upstream tier's group rather than CIDRs. Trap: putting the database in a public subnet or in one AZ.

title: Queue vs topic vs event bus: buffering, fan-out, routing

unit: Determining the lowest cost method of transferring data for a workload to AWS storage
title: Nightly 2 TB from data centre to S3, cheapest path
must_teach: Ingress is free; DataSync over the existing internet link (or existing DX) is cheapest at that volume; Snowball daily fees and DX port fees do not pay back for 2 TB/night unless a DX already exists.
distractor_angles: New Direct Connect violates least-cost (port hours for modest volume); Snowball violates least-cost/ops for nightly recurring; Transfer Family violates least-cost (~$216/month endpoint); S3 Transfer Acceleration adds per-GB fee for a fixed site with adequate bandwidth.

title: Logs hot 30 days, audit 7 years, cheapest valid rule
must_teach: Standard -> Standard-IA at 30 -> Deep Archive at 120+ -> expire at 7 years; reject options that transition before minimum durations.
distractor_angles: Deep Archive at day 45 after IA at day 30 violates chained-minimum constraint (needs 30 days in IA); Glacier Flexible violates least-cost vs Deep Archive when 48 h restore is acceptable; Intelligent-Tiering adds monitoring fee for a known pattern; manual script violates least-ops.

unit: Selecting the correct data lifecycle for storage
title: Versioned bucket bill keeps growing: choose two actions
must_teach: NoncurrentVersionExpiration (or transition) plus AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload; delete markers with no versions are cleaned by ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker.
distractor_angles: Disabling versioning violates recoverability constraint and does not remove old versions; Intelligent-Tiering right service wrong feature (does not delete); S3 Batch delete of current objects violates data-retention; Requester Pays unrelated cost lever.

distractor_angles: Provisioning 5x storage upfront violates least-cost; CloudWatch alarm + manual modify violates least-ops; migrating to Aurora is more change than asked; adding a read replica wrong feature (reads, not disk).

title: Backup strategies and what each one costs
must_teach: Snapshots (EBS, RDS, Aurora) are incremental and billed per changed GB; AWS Backup centralizes schedule + retention + cross-Region/account copy and can move recovery points to a cold tier (min 90-day retention, cold tier only after 8 days warm, ~1/5 price). S3 versioning + replication is a backup for objects; Object Lock/vault lock make it immutable. The cost rule: retention length x change rate drives spend, so set lifecycle-to-cold and expiry rather than keeping every recovery point forever.

unit: Block storage options (HDD vs SSD volume types)
title: EBS volume types by cost: gp3, io2, st1, sc1
must_teach: SSD: gp3 (~$0.08/GB, 3,000 IOPS + 125 MiB/s baseline included, ~20% cheaper than gp2), io2 Block Express for sustained >16,000 IOPS or sub-ms latency (pay per provisioned IOPS). HDD: st1 (~$0.045/GB, throughput-optimized, big sequential reads like logs/EMR) and sc1 (~$0.015/GB, cold, infrequently scanned). HDD volumes cannot be boot volumes and cap at 500/250 IOPS; if the workload is random-I/O, HDD is the wrong cheap answer.

unit: Hybrid storage options (DataSync, Transfer Family, Storage Gateway)
title: Hybrid storage: which service for cache, sync, or protocol endpoint
must_teach: Storage Gateway = keep an on-prem NFS/SMB/iSCSI/VTL interface with S3 behind it (ongoing hybrid access, local cache); DataSync = scheduled or one-off bulk copy on-prem <-> S3/EFS/FSx at ~$0.0125/GB with an agent; Transfer Family = managed SFTP/FTPS/FTP/AS2 endpoint for external partners (~$0.30/hr per protocol, so never for an internal one-time migration). title: Match the access pattern to the storage class and its hidden fees
must_teach: Frequent, unpredictable, or small-object (<128 KB) access -> S3 Standard or Intelligent-Tiering; infrequent but millisecond retrieval -> Standard-IA (or One Zone-IA when data is re-creatable and 99.5% availability is fine); rarely read, minutes-to-hours OK -> Glacier classes. IA classes charge per-GB retrieval ($0.01/GB) and per-request premiums, so data read monthly costs more in IA than in Standard; that break-even (roughly one full read per month) is the exam trap.

unit: AWS storage services with appropriate use cases
title: Cheapest storage service per access pattern: S3 vs EBS vs EFS vs FSx
must_teach: Decision order for cost: object data read over HTTP -> S3 (cheapest per GB, no compute attached); single-instance block with random writes -> EBS; POSIX shared across instances/AZs -> EFS (pay per GB used, no provisioning); Windows SMB/AD, Lustre HPC, ONTAP/ZFS features -> FSx. Trap: EFS per-GB is ~3x S3 and ~3x EBS gp3, so it wins only when shared multi-instance access is a hard requirement.

unit: Storage tiering (cold tiering for object storage)
title: S3 storage class ladder and when to automate it
must_teach: Ladder: Standard -> Standard-IA (30-day min, $0.0125/GB) -> Glacier Instant Retrieval (90-day min, ms access) -> Glacier Flexible (90-day, minutes-hours, free bulk) -> Deep Archive (180-day, 12-48 h, ~$0.00099/GB). Use lifecycle rules when the age-based pattern is known; use Intelligent-Tiering when it is unknown, accepting a per-object monitoring fee ($0.0025/1,000) in exchange for no retrieval fees.

unit: Storage types with associated characteristics (object, file, block)
title: Object vs file vs block: characteristics that drive price
must_teach: Block (EBS): attached to one instance, random read/write at byte level, billed for provisioned GB whether used or not. File (EFS/FSx): shared POSIX/SMB namespace, billed per GB used (EFS) or provisioned (FSx). Object (S3): whole-object PUT/GET over HTTP, no in-place edits, unlimited size, cheapest per GB with request fees. The cost pattern: whenever an app only ever writes whole files and reads them back, moving from EBS/EFS to S3 is the largest saving.

title: Backup (restorable) vs archive (retained): pick the cheaper fit
must_teach: Backup = frequent recovery points with short retention -> AWS Backup / snapshots with lifecycle to cold storage; archive = rarely accessed, long retention -> S3 Glacier Deep Archive with Object Lock / Vault Lock. Tape retirement -> Tape Gateway to Glacier. Trap: keeping full daily snapshots for 7 years instead of moving to Deep Archive.

unit: Data migration service selection (online vs offline)
title: Transfer-time formula: DataSync/DX vs Snow
must_teach: Days = TB x 8 / (Gbps x 0.8 x 86,400/1,000). If the estimate exceeds about a week or the link is shared/unreliable, ship Snowball Edge (210 TB per device); otherwise DataSync over internet/DX. Ingress into S3 is free either way; DX pays port hours, DataSync pays per GB, Snowball pays per job + days.

must_teach: PUT/COPY/POST/LIST cost ~$0.005 per 1,000 and GET ~$0.0004 per 1,000, so millions of tiny objects cost more in requests than storage; batch/aggregate (Kinesis Data Firehose buffering, tar/parquet files, multipart for large objects) and use S3 Batch Operations for bulk actions.
